promptText: Why does a child component re-render whenever its parent re-renders, even if the child's own props haven't changed?
options: React doesn't diff props to decide whether to call a component's function — it re-runs the function on every parent render by default, and only diffs the resulting element tree to decide what to touch in the DOM
React re-renders every descendant because JavaScript garbage collection requires refreshing all closures on each render
Child components subscribe to a global re-render event that fires whenever any component in the app updates
Props changing is the only thing that can trigger any component's re-render
explanation: React calls a component's function again whenever its parent renders, regardless of whether props actually changed — it's only after calling the function that React diffs the resulting elements to decide what DOM work is needed.

promptText: A component wrapped in React.memo still re-renders on every parent render even though the underlying data hasn't logically changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: The parent passes an inline object, array, or arrow function as a prop, creating a new reference every render, which fails memo's shallow Object.is comparison even though the data is logically the same
React.memo only works on class components, not function components
React.memo requires the child to also call useState internally to function correctly
Shallow comparison always returns false for any component with more than one prop
explanation: React.memo compares props by reference; an inline object, array, or arrow function literal created fresh in the parent's JSX is a new reference every render, so the shallow comparison always reports 'changed' and memo never bails out.

promptText: Why is useMemo(() => a + b, [a, b]) typically slower than simply writing a + b directly?
options: The hook still allocates a slot to store the cached value, performs a dependency array comparison every render, and retains a closure — overhead that exceeds the cost of just re-running a trivial addition
useMemo always executes the computation function twice to verify the result is deterministic
useMemo requires an async function and therefore always adds a network round trip
JavaScript engines cannot optimize arithmetic performed inside a useMemo callback
explanation: Memoization is a cache with its own read, write, and memory cost; for a near-free computation like addition, that bookkeeping overhead outweighs whatever it saves, so useMemo should be reserved for genuinely expensive computations or referential-stability needs.

promptText: What is the core mechanism list virtualization libraries use to render 100,000 items without creating 100,000 DOM nodes?
options: They track scroll position, compute which index range is currently visible plus a small overscan buffer, and render only that slice, faking the full scrollable height with a sized spacer element
They convert the entire list into a single canvas element and draw text manually instead of using the DOM
They pre-render all 100,000 items once and then permanently cache them in IndexedDB
They split the list across multiple Web Workers, each rendering a portion of the DOM independently
explanation: A virtualizer keeps a fixed-size window of DOM nodes matching the visible viewport plus overscan, recycling them as the user scrolls, while a spacer element sized to the total content height keeps native scrolling and the scrollbar behaving correctly.

promptText: Why does lazy-loading a component that's needed immediately on page load typically hurt rather than help performance?
options: It adds a network round trip and a loading spinner for content the user needed right away, instead of deferring genuinely non-critical code — split what's deferred, not what's critical
React.lazy components always render twice, doubling the render cost regardless of when they're needed
Suspense boundaries block all other components on the page from rendering until the lazy one resolves, even unrelated ones
Lazy-loaded components cannot use hooks, so critical interactive components would lose functionality
explanation: Code splitting trades an extra network fetch for a smaller initial bundle; that trade only pays off for code the user doesn't need immediately. Lazy-loading critical, immediately-needed content just adds a spinner and latency with no benefit.

promptText: What do LCP, CLS, and INP each measure as Core Web Vitals?
options: LCP measures loading (time to render the largest visible element), CLS measures visual stability (unexpected layout shifts), and INP measures responsiveness (latency from interaction to next paint)
LCP, CLS, and INP are three different ways of measuring the same underlying metric: total page load time
LCP measures JavaScript bundle size, CLS measures CPU usage, and INP measures memory consumption
All three metrics are calculated exclusively from Lighthouse lab data and have no real-user field equivalent
explanation: LCP (loading), CLS (visual stability), and INP (responsiveness, which replaced FID in 2024) are Google's three user-centric Core Web Vitals, each targeting a different dimension of perceived page quality.

promptText: In the "children as a prop" pattern, why does an expensive child subtree avoid re-rendering when its wrapper component's own state changes?
options: The child elements were created by an ancestor component and passed into the wrapper as the children prop, so the wrapper re-running its own function body doesn't recreate them — React reuses the same element objects across the wrapper's re-renders
Children props are automatically wrapped in React.memo by the framework whenever they are passed through more than one component
The wrapper's state update only affects components that are direct DOM children, never React children passed as props
This technique requires manually calling ReactDOM.createPortal to isolate the subtree
explanation: Elements passed into a component as props (including children) were created by whichever ancestor rendered them — the receiving component's own re-render doesn't recreate those element objects, so moving fast-changing state into a wrapper above expensive children isolates the churn without any memoization.

promptText: Why does a slow useEffect callback not show up as a wide bar in the React DevTools Profiler's commit that triggered it?
options: useEffect callbacks run asynchronously after the browser has painted, specifically so they don't block visual updates, so their time appears as a gap before the next commit (or in the browser's own performance timeline) rather than inside the current commit's duration
The Profiler only records effects that are wrapped in useLayoutEffect, and silently drops all useEffect timing data
useEffect callbacks execute on a separate JavaScript thread that the Profiler cannot instrument
Effects always run before the commit phase begins, so their cost is bundled into the previous commit instead
explanation: A commit's duration in the Profiler covers the render and commit phases (including synchronous useLayoutEffect); passive useEffect callbacks are scheduled after paint by design, so a slow one shows up as a gap or a separate task in the Chrome Performance panel, not inside the commit bar.

promptText: An SSR page has excellent LCP but poor INP immediately after load. What's the most likely explanation?
options: The HTML painted quickly because it arrived pre-rendered, but hydration still requires downloading, parsing, and executing the full JS bundle and re-running every component's render logic on the client before event listeners attach — clicks during that window feel unresponsive
INP is only measurable in CSR apps, so any SSR page will always report a poor or undefined INP score
A high LCP score always causes a proportionally worse INP score due to a shared measurement budget
SSR pages cannot have event handlers at all until a full page reload occurs
explanation: SSR solves 'when is content visible' but not 'when is content interactive' — that's still gated on the client-side hydration pass, which walks the whole rendered tree and attaches listeners; a large hydration cost can leave a visually-complete page unresponsive to input for a real, measurable window.

promptText: How does streaming SSR (renderToPipeableStream with Suspense) improve perceived load compared to traditional SSR?
options: It sends the shell and any fast-ready content immediately, then streams in additional HTML for slower Suspense-wrapped sections as their data resolves, instead of blocking the entire response on the slowest data dependency
It compresses the entire HTML response using a more efficient algorithm than traditional SSR
It pre-hydrates every component on the server so no client-side hydration is needed at all
It replaces the need for a CDN by caching the streamed response directly in the browser
explanation: Traditional SSR must fully render the page — including every data dependency — before sending any bytes; streaming SSR flushes the shell and fast content right away and streams in slower Suspense-wrapped sections as they resolve, so TTFB reflects the shell's readiness rather than the slowest fetch.

promptText: A user has an old tab open after a new deploy, and their next lazy-loaded route's chunk file no longer exists on the server. What actually happens, and how do you handle it correctly?
options: The rejected import promise throws during render and propagates to the nearest error boundary, not the Suspense fallback (which only handles the 'still loading' state) — so Suspense must be paired with an error boundary that offers a reload prompt
React automatically detects the stale chunk and silently falls back to re-downloading the entire application bundle
The Suspense fallback displays indefinitely since Suspense treats a failed import the same as a slow one
The browser's Service Worker automatically intercepts and retries the failed request without any application code
explanation: Suspense only handles the 'still loading' case; a rejected chunk-load promise is an ordinary thrown error that must reach an error boundary. Pairing Suspense with an error boundary that offers a reload (fetching the fresh HTML/manifest) is the standard fix for this common post-deploy production bug.

promptText: After splitting one large context into UserContext, ThemeContext, and CartContext, a component that reads only ThemeContext still re-renders too often. What is the likely remaining limitation?
options: Context has no field-level subscription even within one context — if ThemeContext's value is an object with multiple fields, any change to any field re-renders every consumer of that context, regardless of which field the component actually uses
Splitting contexts is purely cosmetic and provides no actual re-render reduction in React
Consumers of a split context must manually call useMemo on every read or the split has no effect at all
React limits apps to a maximum of two context providers before re-render optimization stops working entirely
explanation: Splitting contexts fixes coarse-grained over-subscription across unrelated concerns, but each individual context is still all-or-nothing: any change to its value re-renders every consumer, since Context has no per-field subscription mechanism the way a selector-based store does.

promptText: In a Server Components tree, Page awaits getPageData() before rendering <Sidebar/>, and Sidebar only starts its own independent getSidebarData() fetch once it renders. Both fetches don't depend on each other. What is the precise fix, and why does it work?
options: Kick off both fetches at the same point (e.g., in Page, without awaiting either immediately), pass the resulting promises down as props, and let each component consume its own promise independently — this overlaps the two requests in time instead of running them serially just because of where each component happens to sit in the render tree
Wrap Sidebar in React.memo, which automatically parallelizes any fetch calls inside memoized components
Convert both components into Client Components so their fetches run in the browser instead of the server
There is no fix possible; any two fetches in a Server Component tree must always execute sequentially by design
explanation: The waterfall exists only because Sidebar's fetch is triggered by its own render, which is gated on Page's await finishing first. Starting both fetches together and passing the unawaited promises down decouples request timing from tree position, letting genuinely independent fetches run in parallel.

promptText: A team notices a memoized <Table> component with a custom arePropsEqual comparator that deep-compares a large rows array is not actually faster than an unmemoized version. What is the most likely explanation, and what is the better fix?
options: The deep-equality check itself runs on every render regardless of outcome and can cost more than just re-rendering a modest component would — the better fix is making the rows array reference stable upstream (e.g., via useMemo where it's derived) so the default shallow comparator works correctly, instead of writing a smarter deep comparator
Custom comparators in React.memo are ignored by the reconciler, so the deep-equality function never actually executes
Deep equality checks are always O(1) regardless of array size, so this cannot be the source of any slowdown
The fix is to remove React.memo entirely and instead wrap every row in its own separate component tree with no comparison at all
explanation: A custom deep-equality comparator runs unconditionally on every render, and for a large array can cost more than the render it's trying to avoid. The senior fix is stabilizing the reference at the source so the cheap default shallow comparator works, rather than compensating with a more expensive comparator.

promptText: A dashboard takes 4 seconds to become interactive after a release. The Chrome Performance panel shows a 2-second request waterfall (three independent API calls running serially) followed by a 2-second long task during React rendering, which the Profiler's Ranked view attributes to a new widget doing an unmemoized sort on every parent-triggered re-render. What is the correct fix, and what does this scenario illustrate about performance debugging?
options: Parallelize the three independent fetches (e.g., with Promise.all or by starting them together) and wrap the widget's expensive sort in useMemo keyed to its actual data dependency — the scenario illustrates that a single slow interaction can have multiple independent root causes, not just one bottleneck to find and stop looking
Since the network waterfall accounts for more total time, only the fetches need to be fixed; the render cost is negligible by comparison and should be left alone
The correct fix is to convert the entire dashboard to a fully client-rendered SPA, which would eliminate both the network waterfall and the render cost simultaneously
Because both issues appeared in the same release, they must share one root cause, so fixing the data-fetching pattern alone will also resolve the rendering issue
explanation: The two problems are structurally unrelated (a sequential-fetch waterfall and an unmemoized expensive computation) and both contribute real, separate time to the total delay; a thorough investigation fixes both rather than stopping after finding the first or largest-looking cause.
